extracted.intended_audience: physicists / mathematicians reading Newtonian mechanics (readers of Newton's Principia); scholars of classical mechanics
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted propositions (with corollaries and explanatory material) from a section of Newton's Principia concerning resistance in media, oscillations in a cycloid, motion in fluids, projectile resistance, and efflux of water. Each proposition states physical laws relating resistance, velocity, geometry, and fluid properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXIX (Prob. VII): Resistance in a cycloid with R ∝ v^2
rubrics_metrics.description: Posito quod corpus in Cycloide oscillans resistitur in duplicata ratione velocitatis: invenire resistentiam in locis singulis. (Assuming a body oscillating in a cycloid is resisted in the duplicate ratio of the velocity, find the resistance at each point.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derives that the resistance at a point D is proportional to a difference of hyperbolic areas: resistentia in loco D ad vim gravitatis ut area {OR ÷ OQ} IEF - IGH ad aream PIENM. Shows that if resistance is taken proportional to v^2, one can express resistance via constructed hyperbolic-area relations; includes corollaries: (1) resistance at lowest point C to gravity given by a corresponding area ratio ({OP ÷ OQ} IEF to PINM); (2) maximum resistance occurs when area PIHR is to IEF as OR to OQ (momentum term vanishes); (3) velocities at points are related to resistance (velocitas in dimidiata ratione resistentiæ) and match initial velocity of the same cycloid without resistance. Also notes practical difficulty of calculation under this proposition and motivates the next, more general proposition. Contains detailed geometric construction and limiting-areamoment arguments relating small path elements, increments of resistance, and velocity changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXX (Theor. XXIII): Relation of arc-difference to area of perpendiculars (cycloidal pendulum)
rubrics_metrics.description: Si recta aB æqualis sit Cycloidis arcui quem corpus oscillando describit, & ad singula ejus puncta D erigantur perpendicula DK, quæ sint ad longitudinem Penduli ut resistentia corporis in arcus punctis correspondentibus ad vim gravitatis: dico quod differentia inter arcum descensu toto descriptum, & arcum ascensu toto subsequente descriptum, ducta in arcuum eorundem semisummam, æqualis erit areæ BKaB a perpendiculis omnibus DK occupatæ, quamproxime. (If the straight line aB equals the cycloid arc described by the oscillating body, and perpendiculars DK at each point are proportional to resistance vs gravity, then the difference between total descended arc and subsequent ascended arc, multiplied by the semisum of those arcs, equals (approximately) the area occupied by those perpendiculars.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives a geometric method to relate the loss (difference) of oscillation arc-lengths to the integral of the local resistances (represented by perpendiculars DK). Provides corollaries and approximations useful for practical estimation: if resistance is uniform, DK constant and DK = 1/2 Aa; if resistance ∝ velocity then the figure is approximately an ellipse and gives numeric approximations (e.g., 7/11 Aa to pendulum length), and if resistance ∝ v^2 the figure is approximately a parabola giving other numeric relations (e.g., OV ≈ 3/4 Aa and hence resistance in O to gravity as 3/4 Aa to pendulum length). Also gives the method of approximating the area BKT by symmetric cancellations over oscillation halves and discusses how to use the relation to estimate resistance from measured differences in successive arcs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXXI (Theor. XXIV): Scaling of arc-difference with changes in local resistance
rubrics_metrics.description: Si corporis oscillantis resistentia in singulis arcuum descriptorum partibus proportionalibus augeatur vel minuatur in data ratione; differentia inter arcum descensu descriptum & arcum subsequente ascensu descriptum, augebitur vel diminuetur in eadem ratione quamproxime. (If the resistance of an oscillating body in corresponding parts of the arcs is increased or decreased in a given ratio, the difference between the descended and subsequently ascended arc will increase or decrease in the same ratio approximately.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that the difference in arcs arises from retardation by resistance and therefore scales with the total retardation, which is proportional to the resistance. Corollaries: if resistance ∝ v then the arc-difference is proportional to the total arc; if resistance ∝ v^2 the difference scales as the square of the total arc; generally, if resistance scales as any power of velocity, the arc-difference scales correspondingly in the same manner. Also notes mixed cases (partly ∝ v and partly ∝ v^2) produce additive mixed-scaling in arc-difference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXXII (Theor. XXV): Similarity scaling for two particulate systems (fluids/particles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Si corporum Systemata duo ex æquali particularum numero constent & particulæ correspondentes similes sint, singulæ in uno Systemate singulis in altero, ac datam habeant rationem densitatis ad invicem, & inter se temporibus proportionalibus similiter moveri incipiant ... dico quod Systematum particulæ ille pergent inter se temporibus proportionalibus similiter moveri; & contra. (Two systems of particles equal in number and with corresponding similar particles, with given density ratio and similar motions proportional in time, will continue to move similarly under forces proportional to inverse diameters and to the squares of velocities.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formalizes geometric similarity and dynamical similarity: under the stated proportionality assumptions for particles and forces (accelerating forces ∝ inverse diameters and ∝ v^2), motions remain similar and times scale proportionally. Corollaries derive scaling consequences: if corresponding parts are similar and similarly placed, scaled motions and spaces are described proportionally; this underpins later arguments about how resistance scales between systems (e.g., projectiles in fluids) when geometric, density, and dynamic similarity hold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXXIII (Theor. XXVI): Composite scaling law for resistance of system parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Iisdem positis, dico quod Systematum partes majores resistuntur in ratione composita ex duplicata ratione velocitatum suarum & duplicata ratione diametrorum & ratione densitatis partium Systematum. (Under the same assumptions, the resistance of larger parts of the systems is in the composite ratio of the duplicate ratio of their velocities, the duplicate ratio of their diameters, and the ratio of their densities.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that resistance arises partly from centripetal/centrifugal-type interactions and partly from collisions/reflections; combining these gives resistance ∝ (velocity)^2 × (diameter)^2 × density (for corresponding parts). Corollaries: in elastic (air-like) fluids, a fast projectile is resisted approximately in the duplicate (square) ratio of its velocity; resistance of similar bodies is proportional to the squares of their diameters; very fast bodies experience nearly the same resistance whether fluid particles exert centrifugal repulsions or not; refinements discuss how non-ideal particle interactions (non-maximal elasticity, non-lubricity, particle size/distribution) alter the exact exponent or factor (making resistance deviate from exact v^2 scaling), and how fluid particle properties (size, elastic behavior) affect accuracy of the v^2 law. Nine corollaries discuss consequences for elastic fluids, dependence on particle lubrication, size effects (larger bodies less strictly obey v^2 law), and limits when particle elastic forces arise from other origins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXXIV (Theor. XXVII): Extension to systems where particles contact if highly lubricous
rubrics_metrics.description: Quæ in præcedentibus duabus Propositionibus demonstrata sunt, obtinent ubi particulæ Systematum se mutuo contingunt, si modo particulæ illæ sint summe lubricæ. (The results of the preceding two propositions hold where system particles touch one another, provided those particles are extremely lubricous.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues by limiting process: if inter-particle repulsive forces grow infinitely in approach and vanish rapidly upon recession, and if inter-particle spacing and diffusion ranges are made arbitrarily small, the prior similarity and scaling laws remain valid even when particles contact. Corollaries restate that the composite resistance scaling from Prop. XXXIII holds when fluid particles are extremely lubricous, and again that in such fluids projectiles of given magnitude are resisted in duplicate ratio of velocities. Notes deviation if particles are not extremely lubricous: projectiles slower will face greater resistance than predicted by strict v^2 law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXXV (Theor. XXVIII): Comparative resistance of sphere and cylinder (equal diameters) in a rare elastic medium
rubrics_metrics.description: Si Globus & Cylindrus æqualibus diametris descripti, in Medio raro & Elastico, secundum plagam axis Cylindri, æquali cum velocitate celerrime moveantur: erit resistentia Globi duplo minor quam resistentia Cylindri. (If a sphere and a cylinder of equal diameters move equally and very fast in a rare elastic medium along the cylinder axis, the resistance of the sphere is half that of the cylinder.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives a geometric/kinematic argument based on the effect of fluid particles striking and reflecting from the body; reduces to comparing solid-angle-type solids under certain constructed rectilinear measures, concluding the sphere experiences half the total effect of the cylinder. Scholium: method extends to compare other shapes and to derive shapes (e.g., certain frusta, solids of revolution) that minimize resistance for a given base and height — with explicit geometric constructions for optimal frustum/cone and remarks about applications (ship forms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXXVI (Prob. VIII): Resistance of a sphere moving very fast in a rare elastic fluid
rubrics_metrics.description: Invenire resistentiam corporis Sphærici in Fluido raro & Elastico velocissime progredientis. (Determine the resistance of a spherical body advancing very rapidly in a rare elastic fluid.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructs a hyperbolic-area-based method: chooses proportional constructions CR, CT, CZ, etc., and shows that motion lost by the sphere in traversing a small distance CZ is to its total motion at the start as CT to CR approximately. Uses the result that the sphere's resistance relates to that of an associated cylinder and to mass of fluid reflected; corollaries: (1) given initial speed, one can deduce time to lose a given fraction of motion and thereby get resistance relative to gravity; (2) if fluid particles reflect elastically (maximum reflection), resistance is twice as large as if particles do not reflect at all — so in a non-reflective fluid the sphere would suffer half the resistance computed under maximal reflection; (3) intermediate partial reflectivity gives intermediate resistance; (4) for slow bodies resistance deviates and they lose a larger fraction of motion over CZ than predicted for very fast bodies; (5) knowing resistance for very fast bodies helps infer resistance for slow bodies if the law of decrease of resistance with velocity is known.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXXVII (Prob. IX): Motion of water effluxing from a vessel through an orifice
rubrics_metrics.description: Aquæ de vase dato per foramen effluentis definire motum. (Define the motion of water flowing out from a given vessel through a hole.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that the vessel supports the weight of the whole column of water except the part directly over the orifice; when the obstruction is removed the unbalanced portion of weight accelerates the effluxing water. Quantifies by letting F = area of the orifice, A = head height, P = its weight, AF = quantity, S = space that a freely falling body would describe in time T, V its velocity, and equates the total momentum generated (AF × V) to the momentum of the effluent column. From the algebraic relations obtains the relation between orifice area, head, and efflux velocity (leading to the classical Torricelli-like result via Newton's momentum argument). Concludes with relations between ratios dd:ee and A:2S and between d:e and (1/2)A:S as derived from the momentum balance and geometric substitution.
